n: Victory Museum (Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War)
funding: The museum is a federal state budgetary cultural institution, the Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War 1941 to 1945, run by the Russian state with the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation as its parent body. Its general director is Alexander Shkolnik, who was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022. The museum describes itself as a centre of patriotic education for new generations and for countering falsification of history.
note: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in a building by Anatoly Polyansky with 14,143 square metres of permanent galleries; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.

propaganda.summary: Since April 2022 the federal museum has staged exhibitions such as Ordinary Nazism and Ordinary NATOzism presenting Ukraine's army as heirs of wartime Nazi collaborators, echoing the Kremlin's denazification justification for the invasion.

funding: Patriot Park is the Central Military-Patriotic Park of Culture and Recreation of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, built and funded by the Russian Defence Ministry, which allocated more than 20 billion rubles to it in 2015. It covers 5,414 hectares including a 3,530 hectare military base and hosts the ministry's annual Army forum. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 together with a Defence Ministry general.
note: Conceived by Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu and opened in stages from 2015 to 2016; Putin called it a major component of the system of military-patriotic education for young people.

propaganda.summary: The Defence Ministry created the park in 2015 for military-patriotic education of youth; in August 2023 it displayed Western armoured vehicles captured in Ukraine during the Army-2023 forum, inspected by Dmitry Medvedev.

funding: From 2002 to 2026 the museum was run by the Foundation for Research on Central and Eastern European History and Society, a public foundation chaired by Mária Schmidt and financed by the Hungarian government, which gave it 5.5 billion forints in 2019. On 1 September 2026 the foundation was dissolved and its tasks passed to Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, a company under the Ministry for Social Relations and Culture. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review of the exhibition.
note: Housed at Andrássy út 60, the former Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters; the museum drew millions of visitors over 24 years and is the Hungarian public collection most visited by foreigners.

propaganda.summary: The first Orbán government opened it on 24 February 2002 under Orbán's adviser Mária Schmidt; historians criticised its equation of fascism and communism and its casting of Hungary as a victim of foreign occupiers.

n: Museum of the Second World War
funding: The museum is a state cultural institution supervised and financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. The culture minister dismissed the PiS-appointed director Grzegorz Berendt in March 2024 and appointed Rafał Wnuk, a co-author of the original exhibition. The museum merged with the Westerplatte Museum in 2017 on the order of Culture Minister Piotr Gliński.
note: Opened 23 March 2017 in a 23,000 square metre building with a 40 metre leaning tower by the Kwadrat studio; 601,000 visitors in 2024.

propaganda.summary: In April 2017 the PiS government merged the museum, dismissed director Paweł Machcewicz and installed Karol Nawrocki, who altered the exhibition; from June 2024 the new management reversed those changes, restoring the authors' original vision.

funding: The museum is a public institution of the Ho Chi Minh City government, belonging to the city's Department of Culture and Sports. It is owned by the Vietnamese state and funded from the city budget and ticket income. It has received more than 25 million visitors in 50 years, about 500,000 a year, two thirds of them foreigners.
note: Opened 4 September 1975 at 28 Võ Văn Tần; one in six international visitors to the city tours it.

propaganda.summary: Opened by the new communist authorities on 4 September 1975 as the Exhibition House for US and Puppet Crimes, renamed in 1990 and 1995; anthropologist Christina Schwenkel describes its uncontextualised self-representation of American war crimes.

funding: The museum is a public service unit directly under Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, with its functions set by ministerial Decision 2372/QD-BVHTTDL of 2025. The decision assigns it propaganda and education work on Ho Chi Minh's life, thought and revolutionary ethics, and it manages state-assigned finances and assets and collects fees. It has received more than 40 million visitors, over 10 million of them foreign.
note: Founded by a Party Secretariat resolution of 25 November 1970 and opened 19 May 1990 on Ho Chi Minh's centenary in a lotus-shaped building by Soviet architect Garon Isacovich; holds 130,000 documents and artefacts.

propaganda.summary: Created by Communist Party resolutions of 1970 and 1977 and opened in 1990, the state museum is tasked by ministerial decision with propaganda and education on Ho Chi Minh's thought and revolutionary ideals.

funding: The museum is owned and operated by Kültür A.Ş., the culture company of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, which began construction in 2005 and opened it in January 2009. It is financed by the municipality through Kültür A.Ş. and by ticket sales. Posocco describes it as one of Istanbul's most popular attractions for domestic and foreign tourists.
note: Built at Topkapı beside the point where the Ottomans breached the walls in 1453; opened with praise from Prime Minister Erdoğan after three years of construction.

propaganda.summary: The AKP-run Istanbul municipality's Kültür A.Ş. opened it in 2009 to convey the spirit of the 1453 conquest; Posocco (2018) analyses it as a case of AKP-era museums promoting Ottoman and Islamic nationalism.

funding: The museum is maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, which has been a private religious corporation since 1946 after the Occupation's Shinto Directive abolished state sponsorship of Shinto. The shrine funds it from its own resources and admission fees; it receives no government money. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.
note: Japan's first Western-style museum, opened February 1882 on the shrine grounds; scholars criticise its revisionist account that omits the experiences of China and Korea.

propaganda.summary: Established in 1882 under the Imperial Army and made a state institution of the Army Ministry by imperial decree in 1910, it ran national spiritual mobilisation exhibitions in the 1930s until September 1945.

funding: The building is owned by Roma Capitale, the City of Rome, and run by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a municipal instrumental body founded in 1998 that operates under an annual service contract with the city. Palaexpo also manages the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz and reports one of the highest self-financing rates among Italian cultural bodies. The city's Office for Education and Culture oversees it.
note: Opened 1883 on Via Nazionale to a design by Pio Piacentini; reopened in 2007 after restoration.

propaganda.summary: The National Fascist Party under Dino Alfieri staged the Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista here from 28 October 1932, opened by Mussolini, behind a fasces facade by Libera and De Renzi; nearly four million people attended.

funding: The hall is run by the National Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall Management Office, an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, and funded from the central government budget. The Ministry of Culture directs its transformation under the government's transitional justice policy and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the Ministry of National Defense. The honour guard itself is provided by the military.
note: Construction began 31 October 1976 and the hall opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard is a major tourist attraction.

propaganda.summary: Built 1976 to 1980 to commemorate Chiang Kai-shek with a giant statue and military honour guard; the Ministry of Culture began a transitional justice project in 2017 and removed the guard in 2024.

funding: The site is owned by the Venezuelan state and controlled by the Ministry of Defense and the Bolivarian National Militia, whose headquarters have been there since 2008. The government organises the visits and the Presidential Honour Guard guards the sarcophagus; the staging of the mausoleum was the responsibility of the state. Since 1981 it has had museum status as the Military History Museum.
note: Built 1904 to 1906 in the 23 de Enero district; by 2014 it received about 800 visitors a day and 2,000 at weekends, and acting president Delcy Rodríguez renewed her oath at the tomb on 6 January 2026 after Maduro's capture.

propaganda.summary: After Chávez died in March 2013 the Maduro government turned the barracks of his 1992 coup into his mausoleum and museum, with honour guard, daily cannon salute and state-staged narrative placing him beside Bolívar.

n: National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War
funding: The museum is a Ukrainian state museum with national status granted by presidential decree on 21 June 1996, financed from the state budget under the Ministry of Culture, which renamed it in July 2015 under the decommunisation laws and reports on its decolonisation work. Its director general is Yurii Savchuk. In 2023 the museum replaced the Soviet emblem on the Motherland Monument's shield with the Ukrainian trident.
note: The 102 metre Motherland Monument houses the main exhibition on an 11 hectare site; more than 21 million visitors since 1981.

propaganda.summary: Opened in 1981 by Leonid Brezhnev as the Ukrainian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War, beneath a Motherland statue bearing the Soviet emblem, to commemorate the Soviet war narrative.

funding: The museum is run by the Stiftung Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, a non-profit foundation under civil law funded by annual matching contributions from the Free State of Saxony and the City of Dresden, with further grants from federal bodies, businesses and foundations. Its board of trustees is chaired by Dresden mayor Annekatrin Klepsch with Saxon state minister Barbara Klepsch as deputy. Iris Edenheiser has been director since 2022.
note: Founded 1912 by Odol manufacturer Karl August Lingner; about 220,000 visitors in 2004.

propaganda.summary: From 1933 the museum served Nazi racial ideology as a propaganda machine of racial hygiene, co-producing with NSDAP offices the touring exhibitions Blut und Rasse (1935 to 1938) and Ewiges Volk (1937 to 1939).
